title: Theme and Point of View
bigQuestion: How does who tells a story change what it means?

story.title: One Bike, Two Stories
story.kicker: Two brothers, one blue bike, one dented fender, and two versions of what happened on Saturday.
paragraphs: Here is how Andre, who is eleven, tells it. "The bike is mine. Grandpa gave it to me. Jalen took it without asking while I was at practice. When I got home the front fender was dented and he was acting like nothing happened. I yelled because he never asks. He just takes."

Here is how Jalen, who is nine, tells it. "Andre never even rides that bike. It sat in the garage for two weeks. I asked Mom and she said fine, as long as I stayed on our street. A car door opened and I swerved and hit the curb. I was going to tell him. He yelled before I could say a word."

Their mom heard both versions in the kitchen, one brother talking over the other. She held up a hand. "Both of you just told me a true story," she said. "And neither of you told me the whole one." Andre had not known Mom said yes. Jalen had not known the bike was from Grandpa, who died last year.

Ms. Reyes read both versions to her fourth-graders on Monday, without saying which brother was right. Then she asked, "What did Andre know that Jalen did not? What did Jalen know that Andre did not?" The class made two lists on the board. The lists did not match.

"That," said Ms. Reyes, "is point of view. Every storyteller stands in one spot and sees from there. Your job as a reader is to notice where they are standing." Then she asked the harder question: "What is this story really about? Not the bike. Underneath the bike." Somebody in the back said, "Asking." Somebody else said, "Listening first."
story.think: What is the bike story really about, underneath the bike? Which brother's version did you believe more at first, and why?

lessons.title: Theme Is Not Topic
lessons.mainIdea: The topic is what a story is about on the surface; the theme is the big idea or lesson underneath it.
reading: Ask a kid what the bike story is about. "A bike," she says. True, but that is the *topic*: the subject on the surface. Now ask what the story is really about. "Asking before you take." "Listening before you yell." Those are the *theme*: the big idea the story carries underneath.

Here is a quick test. A topic is usually one or two words: friendship, a dog, a race, a bike. A theme is a whole idea you can say in a sentence: "True friends stay when things get hard." "Slow and steady wins." If you can say it as a sentence about life, not just about this story, it is a theme.

Themes are not written on the page. Nobody in the bike story says "the theme is listening." You build the theme from what happens and what the characters learn. That is why two readers can find slightly different themes in one story. Both can be right, as long as each one can point to the events that support it.

words.d: what a story is about on the surface, usually one or two words
the big idea or lesson about life that a story carries underneath the events

look.title: Sort the Sentences
look.text: Here are four sentences: "A lost puppy." "Even small kids can be brave." "Two sisters." "Telling the truth costs less than hiding it." Two of these are topics and two are themes.
look.prompt: Which two are themes? What makes them different from the other two?

check.q: Which is a theme, not a topic?
choices: Asking first saves a lot of trouble
check.why: A theme is an idea about life you can say in a sentence. The others are subjects.

check.q: Where do you find a story's theme?
choices: You build it from what happens and what characters learn
check.why: Themes are not stated. Readers build them from the events.

check.q: "Friendship" is a
check.why: One word naming a subject is a topic. A theme is a full idea about life.

lessons.title: What the Character Learns
lessons.mainIdea: The fastest way to a theme is to ask what the main character learned, and how that lesson could apply to anyone.
reading: At the start, Andre yells first and asks later. At the end, he finds out Mom said yes and that he had the story wrong. What did Andre learn? Get the facts before you blow up. Turn that into a sentence about life and you have a theme: "Ask before you judge."

This works for almost any story. Find the main character. Find what she believes or does at the beginning. Find how she is different at the end. The gap between those two is the *lesson*. The lesson, stated so it fits anyone, is the theme. Sometimes a character does not learn, and the reader is meant to. The hare in the race never says he was wrong. You still know.

One story can hold more than one theme. Jalen's side of the bike story teaches something too: even when you have permission, tell the person it belongs to. Look for the theme by following the character who changed the most. Then check it against the events. If the events *support* it, keep it.

words.d: what a character comes to understand by the end of a story
to back up an idea with events or words from the text

look.title: A Fable With No Moral Printed
look.text: A young crow found a shiny bottle cap and hid it in a tree. He was so busy guarding it that he skipped every meal his mother brought. By winter he was thin and the cap was still shiny. He gave it to his sister and ate.
look.cite: model text, written for this lesson
look.prompt: What did the crow learn? Say the theme in one sentence that could be about a person.

check.q: What is the quickest way to find a theme?
choices: Ask what the main character learned
check.why: The change in the main character points straight at the theme.

check.q: What did Andre learn in the bike story?
choices: Get the facts before you get angry
check.why: Andre yelled before he knew Mom had said yes. He learned to ask first.

check.q: The hare never admits he was wrong. Can the story still have a theme?
choices: No, a character must state it
Yes, the reader learns the lesson even if the hare does not
Yes, but only if there is a moral printed
check.why: Sometimes the reader is the one meant to learn. The events still teach.

lessons.title: Two Stories, One Theme
lessons.mainIdea: Different stories from different times and places can share a theme, and comparing them shows what each one adds.
reading: The bike story and the tortoise-and-hare fable seem to have nothing in common. One has brothers, one has animals. But line them up. In both, someone is too sure of himself. In both, that person ends up wrong. "Being too sure can cost you" fits both stories. That is a *shared theme*.

To *compare* two stories, ask three questions. What theme do they share? How does each one show it? What is different about the way they show it? The fable makes its point in a race, in a page. The bike story makes it in a kitchen, with real feelings. Same idea, different clothes.

Comparing helps you understand the theme better. The fable shows the cost of being too sure: you lose the race. The bike story shows something the fable skips: being too sure can hurt someone you love. Read two stories on one theme and you see it from two sides.

words.d: a big idea that two or more stories carry
to look at two things side by side and find what is the same and what is different

look.title: Line Them Up
look.text: Story one: a girl practices free throws every day for a month and finally makes the team. Story two: an ant carries crumbs all summer while a grasshopper sings, and the ant has food when winter comes. Make two columns: what is the same, what is different.
look.prompt: What theme do both stories share? What does each one show that the other does not?

check.q: What do the bike story and the tortoise-and-hare fable share?
choices: A theme about being too sure
check.why: In both, someone is too sure and ends up wrong.

check.q: Which question helps you compare two stories?
choices: How does each story show the shared theme?
check.why: Comparing means looking at how each story handles the same big idea.

check.q: Why read two stories with the same theme?
choices: You see the idea from two sides
check.why: Each story adds something the other skips.

lessons.title: First Person, Third Person
lessons.mainIdea: In first person a character tells the story using I and me; in third person a narrator outside the story uses he, she and they.
reading: "The bike is mine. Grandpa gave it to me." Who is talking? Andre, about himself. He uses I, me, my. A story told by a character from inside is in *first person*. You are in that character's head, hearing his thoughts, seeing only what he sees.

Now try: "Andre came home and saw the dent. He felt his face get hot." Nobody in the story is talking. A voice from outside tells it, using he, she, they, and names. That is *third person*. The voice telling the story is the *narrator*. A third-person narrator can often see more than one character.

The quickest test is pronouns. I, me, we, my: first person. He, she, they, his, her: third person. Flip through any book and check the first page. Knowing which one you are reading tells you how much to trust the voice. A first-person narrator only knows what she knows, and she can be wrong.

words.d: a story told by a character inside it, using I and me
a story told by a voice outside it, using he, she and they
the voice that tells a story

look.title: A Famous First Line
look.text: You don't know about me without you have read a book by the name of The Adventures of Tom Sawyer; but that ain't no matter.
look.cite: Mark Twain, Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, 1884
look.prompt: Which pronouns tell you this is first person? What do you already know about the narrator from the way he talks?

check.q: "I ran to the door and pulled it open." Which point of view is this?
check.why: I is a first-person pronoun. A character inside the story is telling it.

check.q: What is a narrator?
choices: The voice that tells the story
check.why: The narrator is whoever is telling it, inside or outside the story.

check.q: Which pronouns signal third person?
check.why: Third person uses he, she, they and names.

lessons.title: What the Narrator Lets You See
lessons.mainIdea: A narrator's point of view controls what you know, so a reader has to notice what the narrator cannot see or chooses not to say.
reading: When Andre tells it, you never hear that Mom said yes. Not because Andre is lying. He does not know. His *point of view* is the spot he stands in, and from that spot, Mom's kitchen is out of sight. What the narrator does not know, you do not know either, unless you look for gaps.

This means a narrator can be wrong without lying. Andre says, "He never asks. He just takes." That is what it looks like from where Andre stands. From Jalen's spot, he asked the right person. Neither one is making it up. A smart reader asks: what can this narrator see? What might be hidden from him?

Narrators also choose what to tell. Jalen says he swerved for a car door. He does not say how fast he was going. Maybe he was going fast. Maybe he was not. When a narrator skips something, notice the *gap*. The gaps are where the rest of the story lives.

words.d: the spot a narrator stands in, which decides what the narrator can know and tell
something a narrator does not know or leaves out

look.title: How Often Each Brother Says I and Me
look.cite: counted for this lesson from the chapter's opening story
look.prompt: Both brothers talk about themselves and about each other. Does either one say what the other brother was thinking? What does that tell you?

check.q: Why does Andre's version never mention that Mom said yes?
choices: Andre does not know it happened
check.why: From Andre's point of view, that fact is out of sight. He cannot tell what he does not know.

check.q: What is a gap in a story?
choices: Something the narrator leaves out or does not know
check.why: Gaps are what the narrator cannot see or chooses not to say.

check.q: Can a first-person narrator be wrong without lying?
choices: No, being wrong is the same as lying
Yes, the narrator only knows what she can see from her spot
check.why: Andre believed Jalen just took the bike. He was wrong, not lying.

lessons.title: One Event, Two Tellers
lessons.mainIdea: Comparing the same event from two characters shows what each one knows, feels and leaves out, and helps you find the fuller story.
reading: Put the two bike stories side by side. Same Saturday, same dent. Andre: taken without asking. Jalen: Mom said yes. Andre: he was acting like nothing happened. Jalen: I was going to tell him. Every line has a match in the other version, and the matches do not agree.

To compare two accounts, make a chart with three columns: what both say, what only the first says, what only the second says. Both brothers agree there is a dent and that Andre yelled. Only Andre mentions Grandpa. Only Jalen mentions Mom. The middle column is what you can be sure of. The side columns are each teller's *bias*, the way his feelings tilt the story.

Bias is not the same as lying. It just means a person tells the parts that matter most to him. Andre's grief for Grandpa makes the bike matter more. Jalen's feeling of being left out makes the two weeks in the garage matter more. When you read two versions, the fuller story is usually both columns put together.

words.d: one person's telling of what happened
the way a teller's feelings tilt the story toward what matters to that teller

look.title: The Three-Column Chart
look.text: Column one, both say: there was a dent; Andre yelled. Column two, only Andre says: Grandpa gave him the bike; Jalen took it without asking him. Column three, only Jalen says: the bike sat unused for two weeks; Mom gave permission; a car door made him swerve.
look.prompt: Which column would Mom trust most? Which fact from a side column changes the story the most when you learn it?

check.q: What goes in the middle column of a comparison chart?
check.why: The middle column holds what both accounts share. That is what you can be surest of.

check.q: What is bias?
choices: Telling the parts that matter most to you
check.why: Bias is a tilt from feelings, not a lie.

check.q: Which fact appears only in Jalen's account?
choices: Mom said he could ride the bike
check.why: Only Jalen knows Mom gave permission. Andre never heard it.

lessons.title: Why the Author Wrote It
lessons.mainIdea: Authors write to entertain, to inform, or to persuade, and knowing the purpose helps you know how to read.
reading: A joke book, a bus schedule, and a poster that says "Recycle!" were all written on purpose, but not the same purpose. The joke book wants to *entertain*. The schedule wants to *inform*. The poster wants to *persuade* you to do something. Every piece of writing has an author's purpose.

Stories are mostly written to entertain, but not only. A fable entertains and also teaches. A story about a kid who moves to Chicago from another country might entertain, and also help readers understand what that feels like. Ask: what does the writer want to happen inside me when I finish?

Purpose changes how you read. If the purpose is to inform, check the facts. If it is to persuade, watch for one-sided arguments. If it is to entertain, relax and enjoy it, but still ask what it is showing you. The bike story was written to make you think about listening. That is a purpose too.

words.d: to give the reader enjoyment: a laugh, a thrill, a good story
to give the reader facts and information
to try to get the reader to believe or do something

look.title: Three Things on the Fridge
look.text: On the fridge: a comic strip cut from the paper, a note that says "Dentist Tuesday 4:00," and a flyer that says "Vote YES for the new playground, it will make our park safer!"
look.prompt: What is the purpose of each one? How can you tell?

check.q: A poster says, "Turn off the lights and save the planet!" What is its purpose?
check.why: It wants you to do something. That is persuading.

check.q: A bus schedule is written mainly to
check.why: A schedule gives facts. Its purpose is to inform.

check.q: Why does knowing the purpose matter?
choices: It tells you the author's name
It tells you how to read: check facts, watch for one side, or enjoy
check.why: You read a fact sheet, an ad and a story differently.

lessons.title: Making an Inference
lessons.mainIdea: An inference is a smart guess that joins a clue in the text with what you already know.
reading: "Andre had not known Mom said yes." The story never says "Andre felt bad about yelling." But you know he did. How? A clue in the text, plus what you know about people. That is an *inference*: a smart guess built from a clue and your own knowledge.

Here is the formula: clue from the text + what I already know = inference. Clue: a kid comes in soaked, dripping on the floor. What I know: rain soaks people. Inference: it is raining outside. You do this all day without noticing. Reading just asks you to do it on purpose.

An inference is not a wild guess. It has to start from a clue on the page. "Maybe Andre is secretly a robot" is not an inference, because nothing in the story points there. "Andre misses Grandpa" is an inference, because the bike was Grandpa's and Grandpa died last year. The clue is what makes it fair.

words.d: a smart guess made from a clue in the text plus what you already know
a detail in the text that points toward something the text does not say

look.title: Read the Room
look.text: You walk into the kitchen. Two chairs are knocked over. A plate is on the floor in pieces. Your brother is sitting on the counter with the dog on his lap, and the dog's tail is wet with something red.
look.prompt: What do you infer happened? Which clues did you use? What do you know that helped?

check.q: What two things make an inference?
choices: A clue from the text plus what you already know
check.why: Clue plus knowledge equals inference.

check.q: A kid walks in soaked and dripping. What is a fair inference?
check.why: The clue is wet clothes. What you know is that rain soaks people.

check.q: Why is "Andre is secretly a robot" not an inference?
choices: Nothing in the text points to it
check.why: An inference has to start from a real clue on the page.

lessons.title: Backing Up Your Guess
lessons.mainIdea: A good inference comes with its evidence attached: the clue you used and the reasoning that connects it.
reading: In class, Maya says, "Jalen felt guilty." Ms. Reyes asks, "How do you know?" Maya says, "He says 'I was going to tell him.' You only say that when you know you should have said something already." That is an inference with its *evidence* attached. She gave the clue and she explained it.

Use this frame: "I think ___ because the text says ___, and I know that ___." Here is one. I think Jalen felt guilty. The text says he was going to tell Andre. I know people only promise to tell when they feel they owe it. Three parts: the guess, the clue, the *reasoning*.

When you cannot fill in the clue, drop the inference. When you can, you are doing what good readers do: reading what the page says, and also what it means. That is the whole point of reading between the lines. The words are the same for everyone. The meaning is what you build from them.

words.d: the clue from the text that supports an inference
the explanation of how the clue leads to the inference

look.title: The Empty Lunch Bag
look.text: Every day Sam brought a lunch bag to school, and every day at noon he put it, still folded flat, back in his backpack and went out to the yard. On Friday his teacher started leaving a granola bar on his desk.
look.cite: model text, written for this lesson
look.prompt: What do you infer about Sam? What do you infer about the teacher? Give the clue for each.

check.q: Which part is missing from "I think Jalen felt guilty"?
check.why: An inference needs a clue from the text and an explanation attached.

check.q: What is reasoning?
choices: The explanation of how the clue leads to the guess
check.why: Reasoning connects the evidence to the inference.

check.q: You have a guess but cannot find any clue for it. What should you do?
choices: Drop the guess or find a real clue
check.why: An inference without a clue is just a guess. Find one or let it go.

review.q: "Two brothers and a bike" is the story's
review.why: That is the surface subject, the topic. The theme is the idea underneath.
A theme is an idea about life you can say in a sentence.

review.q: "She grabbed her coat and ran." Which point of view?
review.why: She is a third-person pronoun. A voice outside the story is telling it.

review.q: Why can a first-person narrator be wrong without lying?
choices: The narrator only knows what he can see from his spot
review.why: Andre did not know Mom said yes. He told the truth as he saw it.

review.q: Comparing two accounts, what can you be surest of?
choices: What only the first teller says
review.why: What both accounts share is the firmest ground.

review.q: A flyer says, "Join the library club, it is the best club in school!" Its purpose is to
review.why: It is trying to get you to do something.

choices: a fact stated on the page
a smart guess from a clue plus what you know
review.why: Clue from the text plus your knowledge equals an inference.

review.q: "I think Sam has no lunch because his bag is always flat." Which part is the evidence?
review.why: The flat bag is the clue from the text. The rest is the guess.
